topic_title: The Library That Vanished in a Single Afternoon

slides.headline: 700,000 scrolls. One afternoon. Zero survivors.
slides.body: The Library of Alexandria held the largest collection of knowledge the ancient world had ever assembled — and most of it disappeared so completely that historians still argue over how.

slides.headline: Built to hold everything humanity knew
slides.body: Founded under the Ptolemies around the 3rd century BC, the library's mandate was total: acquire a copy of every book that existed, in every language, by any means necessary.

slides.headline: Not one fire. At least four.
slides.body: Caesar's war in 48 BC, a 3rd-century civil war, a 4th-century religious purge, and a 7th-century conquest each get blamed — the truth is the collection was gutted in stages, not a single dramatic night.

slides.headline: We know it existed mostly by its footnotes
slides.body: Ancient writers like Strabo and Galen reference works and catalogs that no longer exist anywhere — citations pointing at a void, the closest thing history has to a paper trail for what was lost.

slides.headline: Every empire since has tried to rebuild it
slides.body: From the Library of Congress to the Internet Archive, the same impulse recurs: centralize all knowledge in one place — and expose it to the same single point of failure every time.

slides.headline: The archive always survives the empire that built it — until it doesn't.
slides.body: Follow for the histories institutions would rather you forgot.
